title: Saw a 45-degree mitre through a picture-frame moulding in a mitre box
instruction: Saw the moulding right through at its pencil line in the mitre box's 45-degree slot, with the moulding against the box's back fence. Leave the saw standing back in its rest, the cut moulding lying on the table in front of the box and both arms back where they started.
context: Picture framers and carpenters cut mitred corners in a mitre box: the moulding has to stay against the back fence at its mark while the backsaw works in the angled slot, and the saw's strokes drag a moulding nobody holds along the box.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A brown beech mitre box, fixed: a plywood base board 1.5 cm thick, from 29.7 to 40.3 cm forward and from 15 cm right to 28 cm left of the centre line, and on it a front wall and a back fence, each 1.5 cm thick and 5 cm tall, running from 15 cm right to 8 cm left, with a 6 cm wide channel between them (its back fence's face 38 cm forward). Saw slots cut through both walls: two at 45 degrees crossing the channel's middle 5 cm right of the centre line, and one at 90 degrees 3 cm left of it. (2) On the table in front of the box, a length of black-lacquered pine picture-frame moulding (94 g), 34 cm long, 2.6 cm wide and 2.2 cm tall, with a gold lip along its front edge, lying along the box 21.5 cm forward, from 8.3 cm right to 25.7 cm left of the centre line; a white pencil line crosses its top at 45 degrees 5 cm from its right end. (3) To the right, a backsaw (160 g): a fine-toothed steel blade (about 15 teeth per inch) 24 cm long and 5 cm deep with a brass back and a turned rosewood handle in line with it, standing teeth down in a beech saw rest (two V-blocks under the blade and a V-cradle under the handle) 21 cm right of the centre line, the blade running forward from 26 to 50 cm, the handle reaching back toward the arms. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged from the whole trial. The moulding is at the mark when its pencil line lies within 1 cm of the 45-degree slot along the box, its back face within 6 mm of the fence, turned less than 4 degrees and lying on the box's floor; it has been laid there once it stays so for 0.5 s. The saw is back in its rest when it stands within 2 cm of where it started, within 1.2 cm of its height and turned less than 10 degrees from it; the cut moulding is out on the table when it lies on the table in front of the box's base board. 1.0: cut through, the saw back in its rest, the cut moulding out on the table and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start), at the end; 0.75: cut through; 0.5: a kerf at least 11 mm deep (half the moulding's 22 mm height); 0.25: the moulding laid at the mark; else 0.0. In a real trial the cut is measured afterwards. It counts only where it crosses the moulding within 1 cm of the pencil line, at 45 degrees (plus or minus 4) to its edge, as a cut through the slot with the moulding at its mark does. Kerf depth is measured with a caliper's depth rod from the moulding's top face to the deepest point of the kerf. Cut through means the offcut has come free along the kerf, sawn over the moulding's full height and width; an offcut snapped or torn off with uncut fibres is not cut through, and the kerf's sawn depth scores instead. In simulation the wood is not cut (see fidelity) and kerf depth is counted in strokes. A stroke is the saw, in the slot (turned within 8 degrees of it, leaning less than 12 degrees, within 9 mm of its line, its teeth within 7 mm above and 8 mm below the bottom of the cut), pushed 3 cm along it while the moulding lies at the mark and moves no more than 4 mm. Each stroke deepens the cut 2.875 mm: four strokes (11.5 mm) earn 0.5, and the eighth (23 mm) frees the offcut. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the saw and both pieces of the moulding still.
reset_notes: Lay the moulding back in one piece on the table in front of the box, and stand the saw back in its rest, teeth down, handle toward the arms.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the wood is not cut. Kerf depth is counted in 3 cm strokes (2.875 mm each; the 8th frees the offcut), a stand-in, as real depth per stroke varies: real trials measure the kerf. The teeth ride on a hidden plate in the moulding that steps down per stroke and drags it by friction; a fixed joint joins the pieces until then. The saw's weight sits near its handle; box, rest fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
